title: Formal banking access coexists with unequal nonbank substitution and weak observed switching after fraud
source_unit: Federal Reserve Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking adult respondent, 2025; published banking and fraud tables

observations.period: 2025 SHED; bank account ownership and overdraft

denominator.unit: published percentage base among all adults

unbanked_under_25000.unit: percent of adults with family income below $25,000

unbanked_100000_plus.unit: percent of adults with family income of $100,000 or more

paid_overdraft_fee_banked.unit: percent of adults with a bank account who paid an overdraft fee in the prior 12 months

paid_overdraft_fee_low_income_banked.unit: percent of banked adults with family income below $25,000

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published bank-account and overdraft estimates; subgroup denominators and banked-adult conditions are retained separately.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported cross-sectional measures do not identify account quality, fees beyond overdraft, authentication access, balances, or whether formal account status provided usable payment access.
observations.subgroup: All adults; family-income groups; banked adults for overdraft measures.
observations.counterinterpretation: An unbanked status may reflect preference, household-spouse account structure, recent transition, or access constraints; an overdraft fee can reflect a short-term liquidity event rather than persistent account failure.

observations.period: 2019 to 2025; nonbank check-cashing or money-order use

denominator.unit: published percentage base among all adults; banked/unbanked subgroup comparisons use all-adult groups

crypto_transaction_unbanked.unit: percent of unbanked adults using cryptocurrency for a financial transaction

crypto_transaction_banked.unit: percent of banked adults using cryptocurrency for a financial transaction

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published nonbank transaction and cryptocurrency-use estimates, retaining account-status conditional universes and the 2019 comparison.
observations.uncertainty: Nonbank use is not a direct measure of exclusion or harm; the survey does not identify transaction price, travel/time burden, reliability, or whether a bank alternative was available.
observations.subgroup: All adults, banked adults, unbanked adults, and cryptocurrency users by account status.
observations.counterinterpretation: Nonbank providers may be convenient or chosen for a specific transaction; falling use since 2019 does not establish improved bank access or reduced need.

observations.period: 2025 SHED; non-credit-card fraud loss, recovery, and response

denominator.unit: published conditional bases among adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud; method-specific items have separate valid universes

lost_money.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud

some_money_not_recovered.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud

median_loss_before_recovery.unit: US dollars among adults who lost money

median_loss_after_recovery.unit: US dollars among adults who lost money

communicated_with_financial_provider.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud

changed_bank_or_financial_provider.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud

reported_to_authority_or_credit_bureau.unit: percent of adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published fraud-loss, recovery, provider-contact, reporting, and bank-change estimates; payment-method and recovery measures allow distinct valid-answer universes.
observations.uncertainty: The figures concern the most recent reported fraud and are self-reported; they do not identify provider liability, dispute success, timing, repeat use, or whether changing providers was feasible or protective.
observations.subgroup: Adults experiencing non-credit-card fraud, with payment-method and response-condition subgroups.
observations.counterinterpretation: A bank change may reflect ordinary life change or a preferred alternative rather than a remedy failure; contacting a provider can produce recovery without switching, while non-switching can reflect satisfaction, inertia, or lack of alternatives.

related_sources.claim: The companion credit chapter supplies credit-card ownership, balance-carrying, and repayment context.
related_sources.access_boundary: Credit use and bank-account access are distinct response surfaces.

related_sources.claim: The income-and-expenses chapter supplies price adaptation, outside support, and budget-margin context.
related_sources.access_boundary: Budget adaptation does not identify a specific provider or fraud episode.

boundary: This record establishes unequal formal banking access, nonbank substitution, fraud recovery burden, provider contact, and reported switching in 2025. It does not establish a causal account or overdraft effect, provider responsibility, verified recovery, consumer welfare, trust change, or practical exit. Access, substitution, recovery, and switching remain separate stages.
